title: How to Evaluate Voice AI for Multi-Step Inbound Support Calls
summary: Evaluate voice AI for multi-step inbound support calls with scenario-based pilot tests, workflow checks, CRM fit, and context-preserving transfers.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Run scored pilot calls based on your inbound queue, not just vendor demos. Include callers who change intent, raise multiple issues, fail verification, or need escalation.
- Score whether voice AI agents follow guardrails and choose the right decision path. Keep the recording and decision trace so reviewers can explain each result.
- Test phone-system and CRM connections in your environment. During warm transfers, check what context reaches the human agent and what happens when no one answers.
- Set pass/fail thresholds against your own support requirements. This guide provides an evaluation framework, not a vendor ranking. See the[vendor comparison](https://sigmamind.ai/blog/inbound-call-automation-comparison) ,[workflow guide](https://sigmamind.ai/blog/inbound-voice-ai-workflows-human-handoff) , and[warm-transfer explainer](https://www.sigmamind.ai/blog/warm-transfer) for related detail.


## Why spec sheets and demos miss multi-step inbound complexity


A scripted demo shows how a voice AI agent handles a planned request, but it cannot show how the agent responds when a caller changes course. A caller might ask about an order, raise a billing dispute after hearing the answer, and then request a person. The agent must keep track of both issues, use the right account information, and recognize when it should stop trying to resolve the call.


Feature checklists leave similar questions open. A vendor may list CRM access, caller verification, and human transfer, but the list does not show whether the agent verifies a caller before revealing account details or passes useful context to a human. Your phone-system configuration and support policies also determine which actions the agent can take.


Use anonymized inbound calls to build pilot scenarios, then give each product the same scenarios, permissions, and tool conditions. Review recordings and action traces to see how each agent handled the call.


## Building a scored test-call set that mirrors real inbound traffic


Turn anonymized call patterns into scenario cards that state what the caller knows, the initial request, what changes during the call, the information the agent may access, and the actions it may take. Draw those patterns from recent logs and complaint records, especially calls that changed direction or ended in a transfer.


Use these scenarios to test distinct decisions and safeguards.


- **Mid-call intent switch.** A caller starts with an order-status question, then asks to dispute a charge. Check whether the voice AI agent recognizes the new request without losing the first one.
- **Multiple issues.** A caller asks about a missing delivery and an address change. Check whether the agent keeps the two requests separate and records which one remains unresolved.
- **Tool failure.** A lookup fails after the caller has provided details. Check whether the agent avoids inventing an answer and follows your approved fallback.
- **Caller verification.** A caller requests account-specific information before completing verification. Check whether the agent withholds protected details and resumes the request after successful verification.
- **Sensitive request.** A caller describes a billing dispute or asks the agent to make a promise it cannot authorize. Check whether the agent stays within the permitted response.
- **Escalation trigger.** A caller asks for a person, becomes frustrated, or reaches a case your policy reserves for staff. Check whether the agent transfers the call at the required point.


Before each run, define the expected outcome and any required intermediate steps, such as verification before disclosing protected account information or making an account change. Include a few variations drawn from the same call pattern, such as a caller who changes their mind after a failed lookup. Run the same cards against each product under comparable conditions so reviewers can distinguish repeatable behavior from a single good call.


For every attempt, save the recording, transcript, tool-call trace, configuration, and final outcome under your data-handling rules. If a product cannot provide a trace, record that evidence gap. Note where the agent changed paths, what information it used, and whether a person had to repair the interaction. Reviewers can then score the agent’s actions as well as its final answer.


## Scoring the pilot and setting your own pass/fail bar


Score each pilot call against the outcome it was supposed to reach, then score how the voice AI agent got there. A call can end with the right answer even if the agent made an unauthorized tool call or skipped verification. Record task completion, tool-call correctness, verification, escalation, and conversation naturalness separately so a successful outcome does not conceal an unsafe path.


Give reviewers the same rubric and available evidence for every call. Mark a criterion unverified when the evidence needed to score it is unavailable rather than treating missing records as a pass. For each dimension, define what a full pass, partial pass, and failure look like before the pilot starts. Tool-call correctness should cover the chosen function, the data sent to it, and what the agent did when the function failed. Verification should cover whether the agent withheld protected information until the caller passed the required check. Score escalation against the scenario’s trigger, including whether the agent transferred a call it could not safely resolve. Score conversation quality and answer accuracy separately. For quality, note repeated questions, interruptions, and ignored corrections. For accuracy, compare account-specific answers with the authorized data available during the call and record claims the evidence cannot verify.


Have two reviewers score a sample of calls independently using the recording, transcript, tool-call trace, and outcome. When their scores differ, record the disputed moment and settle how the rubric applies before scoring the remaining calls. Keep critical failures visible rather than averaging them into an overall score.


Set pass/fail thresholds against your existing contact center QA requirements and the risks of each call type. A billing-dispute scenario may need a different escalation rule than a store-hours question. Ask what a vendor’s reported accuracy percentage measures and how it was tested. Treat it as a vendor claim, not a result from your pilot. Without your own scenarios, scoring rules, and call evidence, that percentage cannot tell you how the agent will handle your inbound traffic.


## Evaluating workflow control, guardrails, and auditability


Your operations staff should be able to use a call’s decision trace to reconstruct why the agent called a tool, chose a branch, or escalated. In the pilot, ask each vendor to replay the same multi-step call and show the tool inputs, branch conditions, and decisions in order. Compare the intended route in the workflow diagram with the route recorded in the call’s decision trace.


Test whether guardrails stop unauthorized actions rather than merely asking the agent to avoid them. For example, have an unverified caller request an account change, then check whether the workflow blocks the tool call before the request reaches the account system. SigmaMind AI’s[workflow guide](https://sigmamind.ai/blog/inbound-voice-ai-workflows-human-handoff) describes Tool Action and Branch nodes that can use session variables or external API data. Treat those as workflow options, not proof that an unverified caller is blocked. Ask SigmaMind AI to show how verification gates and access controls are configured, then test whether they block the action in your deployment.


Ask each vendor what call logs, decision traces, and configuration records it can provide, then collect comparable evidence for every pilot call. Record any gaps in what reviewers can inspect. Ask your operations staff to explain a disputed call path from the available records without vendor assistance. Ask SigmaMind AI to identify documentation for the call records, per-node decisions, and export options available in the proposed configuration, then demonstrate them in the pilot. Confirm those details in the pilot rather than treating an architecture diagram as evidence.


## Testing phone-system and CRM fit in your own environment


An integration listing cannot tell you whether voice AI will work with your phone system and CRM configuration. With appropriate test accounts and permissions, run an inbound pilot call through the number routing, agent desktop, and CRM configuration you plan to use in production. Record where the call connects, whether the intended customer record opens, and whether an authorized update reaches the right fields.


Check the connection method before testing call behavior. Ask each vendor whether your deployment uses SIP or PBX connectivity, a direct CCaaS connection, or another route. Confirm whether you must buy a new number or can bring an existing one. Ask SigmaMind AI for current documentation covering number options, SIP connectivity, and whether VICIdial or Five9 connectivity is available for your proposed deployment. Those documented options do not establish that your specific route, CRM screen pop, or data write-back will work without configuration.


Assign ownership for every connection you test. Ask the vendor to point to current documentation that separates built-in behavior from work your telephony or CRM administrator must complete. Then place a call, open the matching customer record, and attempt an authorized update. Save the call log, routing evidence, and CRM record before and after the call so reviewers can distinguish a connection failure from a field-mapping or permission error.


If your phone environment uses Five9, NICE CXone, Genesys, or Talkdesk, ask the relevant provider for current connection requirements and test the proposed route in your pilot. A third-party comparison cannot establish that your specific configuration will work.


## Proving warm transfer and no-answer fallback actually work


Run a handoff test after a caller changes their request and the voice agent needs to escalate. Ask the receiving agent what they heard before showing them the transcript. Compare that account with the recording. If the proposed transfer uses a private whisper, check whether it identifies the caller’s current request and why the call was escalated. Check separately whether the receiving agent gets the authorized details needed to continue without asking the caller to repeat them.


SigmaMind AI’s[warm-transfer explainer](https://www.sigmamind.ai/blog/warm-transfer) describes a private whisper as one way to give the receiving agent context while the caller waits. Check the context-sharing method in each proposed configuration rather than assuming every warm transfer uses a whisper. If the proposed transfer can play an empty or placeholder whisper, test whether the receiving agent still gets usable context through another channel. Do not count a connected call as a successful context-preserving handoff unless the receiving agent gets usable context.


Inspect the agent desktop separately. Record which structured fields actually arrive, including intent, relevant variables, and caller responses. Check whether those fields match the conversation and give the human agent enough information to continue. Ask SigmaMind AI which structured fields its proposed handoff can send, then test which fields reach your receiving system. A spoken summary does not prove that the CRM received usable data.


Repeat the call when no one answers the transfer. Ask SigmaMind AI which transfer retries and no-answer fallback routes its proposed configuration supports. Before the pilot, agree on a retry limit and fallback destination that the configuration can support. Then check where the caller goes, what context follows them, and whether the call record shows the failed attempt. Score the answered transfer and no-answer path separately.


## Assigning pilot roles and resolving failures


Before the pilot, assign scenarios and acceptance rules to the operations lead, scoring to the QA reviewer, and connection checks to your phone-system and CRM administrators.


Run comparable scenario sets against each shortlisted product in your environment. Choose repetitions based on call volume, consequence of error, and variation between attempts. Add calls when results differ or a serious failure needs retesting, and record the number of runs for each scenario.


When a call fails, have QA and operations identify the disputed moment in the recording and trace. Ask the phone-system and CRM administrators to check the route, permissions, field mapping, and handoff records before attributing the failure to the product, configuration, or an unresolved cause.


## Reusable inbound pilot scorecard


Copy the table for each product and enter the expected behavior before testing. For each row, record a pass, partial pass, or failure, its severity, and the call evidence behind the result. Set any automatic-fail rules and overall acceptance threshold before reviewing results.


Copy the scorecard for each scenario and attempt. After each run, enter the observed result and note any missing evidence.

## FAQs


-


**How many test calls are enough?** Run every scenario in the scorecard and repeat cases where errors would have serious consequences or behavior varies between attempts. Record the run count for each scenario. Resolve reviewer disagreements against the recording and rubric, then repeat a call if its outcome remains unclear.


-


**How should you score conversation quality?** Have reviewers mark specific moments when the agent interrupts, pauses awkwardly, misreads a correction, or makes the caller repeat information. Use the same rubric for every vendor, and review the recording when scores differ.


-


**What counts as a critical failure?** Set that rule before testing. Unauthorized disclosure, an action taken without required verification, or failure to escalate a sensitive request may warrant an automatic fail. A recoverable pause or awkward phrase may warrant a minor deduction.


-


**How do you separate vendor capability from your configuration choices?** Record the configuration used for each call alongside the recording and decision trace. When a call fails, check whether the platform lacked the needed control or the pilot configured that control incorrectly. Correct configuration errors and rerun the same scenario before judging the vendor.


-


**Should IT or operations own the pilot?** Operations should lead the pilot because it defines the call scenarios and acceptance criteria. QA should score the calls, while telephony and CRM administrators verify connections, data handling, and handoffs in the planned environment.


## Keep the scorecard for the next evaluation


Keep the scenarios, scoring rules, configuration records, and call evidence after you choose a product. Reuse them after a model upgrade or when evaluating another vendor, and log scenario changes so later scores remain interpretable. Apply the pass/fail thresholds you set for your own calls rather than substituting a vendor’s performance claim.
